paper.title: Hyperband: A Novel Bandit-Based Approach to Hyperparameter Optimization

settings.name_in_paper: Pure-exploration non-stochastic infinite-armed bandit (NIAB), infinite horizon
unmapped: Each arm is a deterministic (non-stochastic) loss sequence l_{i,k} converging to a limit nu_i; the k-th pull reveals l_{i,k}
Arm limits nu_i drawn i.i.d. from an unknown bounded CDF F; learner may draw new arms at will
Convergence rate governed by unknown envelope function gamma(j) = sup_i |l_{i,j} - nu_i|
settings.definition_quote: Each ``arm'' in the NIAB game is associated with a sequence that is drawn randomly from a distribution over sequences. If we ``pull'' the $i$th drawn arm exactly $k$ times, we observe a loss $\ell_{i,k}$. At each time, the player can either draw a new arm (sequence) or pull a previously drawn arm an additional time. There is no limit on the number of arms that can be drawn.

settings.name_in_paper: Non-stochastic best-arm identification with a fixed set of n arms (Successive Halving)
unmapped: Arms are deterministic loss sequences converging to limits nu_i; deviation bounded by envelope gamma
Budget B and number of arms n given as input; in finite-horizon version the maximum resource R is known
Arm means nu_i drawn i.i.d. with P(nu_i - nu_* <= eps) = c_1^{-1} eps^beta (beta-parameterization)

settings.name_in_paper: NIAB, finite horizon (R finite and known)
unmapped: Deterministic converging loss sequences, limits drawn i.i.d. from unknown F
Maximum resource R with gamma(R)=0 is finite and known to the learner
settings.definition_quote: We separate these two settings into the \emph{finite horizon} setting where $\Rmax$ is finite and known, and the \emph{infinite horizon} setting where no bound on $\Rmax$ is known and it is assumed to be infinite.

source.label: thm:hyperband_infinite_main
source.quote: For any $T \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\hat{\imath}_T$ be the empirically best-performing arm output from  \succhalv from the last round $k$ of \ouralg ... after exhausting a total budget of $T$ from all rounds, then $\nu_{\hat{\imath}_T} - \nu_* \leq c \left( \frac{ \overline\log(T)^3 \overline\log(\log(T)/\delta) }{T} \right)^{1/\max\{\alpha,\beta\}}$ for some constant $c = \exp(O(\max\{\alpha,\beta\}))$ where $\overline\log(x) = \log(x )\log\log(x)$.

results.notes: Theorem does not explicitly write 'with probability 1-delta' but delta is fixed and proof is on a probability 1-delta event; recorded as high probability. T is the total budget (pulls). Paper remarks uniform-allocation variant gives exponent 1/(alpha+beta) (not a formal statement).

source.label: thm:hyperband_infinite_alt
source.quote: Fix $\delta \in (0,1)$ and $q \in (1/K,1)$ and let $z_q = \log( q^{-1} ) (\Delta_{ \lceil \max\{2,q K\} \rceil }^{-\alpha}  + \frac{ 1}{q K} \sum_{i=\lceil \max\{2,q K\} \rceil}^K \Delta_i^{-\alpha} )$. Once $T = \widetilde{\Omega}\left( z_q \log( z_q ) \log( 1/\delta) \right)$ total pulls have been made by \ouralg we have $\widehat{\nu}_T - \nu_* \leq \Delta_{\lceil\max\{2,qK\}\rceil}$ with probability at least $1-\delta$

results.notes: Sufficient number of pulls (upper bound on sample complexity) to get within Delta_{ceil(max{2,qK})} of best, hiding loglog factors. Here K is number of atoms of F.
